As an avid player of Civ IV, I get what you are saying, but to use that game as an indicator of real life is more disturbing than anything for an average citizen.

The "best" model of governance for a state that wants to provide endless wealth and prosperity for citizens in Civ IV is a somewhat dystopia: free speech, emancipation, free religion, as long as you can stomach the police state and complete state ownership of property.

In Civ IV, the message is that the average citizen has no winning conditions.

I think that's a good way of putting it. I think the key difference between in-game governance and real-life governance is that in-game, people are simply the means to an end. In real life, we try to make government the means to our ends. RTS games typically don't have that kind of "push back" from the in-game populations. It might be interesting to see how well we could manage a game that kept those kinds of parameters in mind.

Civ IV does have "war weariness," unhappiness from slavery and drafting, demands for emancipation, and desertions from the military if the economy is in the shitter (there are others but those are the most predominant typically). It could be argued the scale in which those are truly representative of real life, but to me, that was Sid Meier's way of saying that the masses are easily placated even in the worst of conditions, and that a State has to really be fucking up for the push back to be truly effective.
Could be that's life in a nutshell as well :) either way, it sounds like an interesting game mechanic.
